rationale: B wins because it is more disciplined about what must be proven before anyone pitches this. Its line, "the pharmacy chain's name — without it this angle cannot be pitched at all," is exactly the kind of brake a founder needs. A has strong shapes, but "Warby Parker is testing whether a pharmacy aisle sells glasses better than its own stores" invents a bake-off the update does not support. That is not seasoning; that is adding an ingredient.
gaps_in_A: "Warby Parker is testing whether a pharmacy aisle sells glasses better than its own stores" invents a comparison. The fact block says pharmacy-chain pilot, not that Warby is testing pharmacy against owned stores.

"Warby Parker bets its future on the stores it was built to disrupt" overstates the evidence. Forty new stores and 300-plus total stores support a retail-strategy story, not a whole-company future bet.

"the profitability claim and the exam-revenue rollout are being announced together" is too tidy. The update says Warby recently reached profitability and is expanding exams; it does not prove those were packaged as one disclosure.
The set admits "Without a name, the counterposition angle can't be pitched as written" but still keeps the pharmacy angle as if it is ready. That should be gated harder.
gaps_in_B: "Warby Parker was the canonical example of that thesis" leans on outside reputation, not the supplied update. It may be true, but this exercise rewards traceable facts, not memory swagger.
"the death of a retail thesis" is too grand. One 40-store expansion can challenge a thesis; it does not bury it with a tiny violin.
"a newly profitable public company is funding a 40-store buildout" assumes capital-allocation mechanics the update does not provide. Ask for capex; do not smuggle it in as fact.
"pharmacy chains' fight to reinvent the front of store" imports an outside trend peg. Useful if verified, but it is not in the fact block.
